blocks.text: 1. The Machine Learning Workflow

AI Versus ML Versus Deep Learning, the previous topic, set this course's actual scope clearly: traditional Machine Learning, not Deep Learning or non-learning AI. Every real Machine Learning project built within that scope follows roughly the same end-to-end workflow, regardless of the specific algorithm or problem involved.

This workflow is a repeatable sequence of stages, each one covered in its own dedicated module later in this course. This topic previews that full sequence at a high level, before this course dives into any single stage in genuine depth, giving a clear map of where everything that follows actually fits.
2. The Full Sequence

blocks.alt: The workflow moves from defining the problem through collecting data, exploring it, engineering features, training, and deploying

blocks.text: The full Machine Learning workflow moves through seven broad stages. It starts with defining the problem, then collecting data, then exploring and understanding that data, then preparing and engineering features from it.

From there, it moves to choosing and training a model, evaluating that model, and finally deploying and monitoring it once it is genuinely ready for real-world use. Each of these seven stages gets its own dedicated coverage across the modules that make up the rest of this course.

blocks.text: 3. Defining the Problem

blocks.alt: A vague business ask becomes a concrete, measurable problem

blocks.text: This connects directly back to Supervised, Unsupervised, and Reinforcement Learning, all covered earlier in this module. Defining the problem means deciding, right at the start, what type of Machine Learning actually fits the situation at hand, a decision that shapes essentially every stage that comes after it.

Is a correct, known answer already available to learn from? Is the goal predicting a number, or a category? Or does the problem instead involve a sequence of decisions unfolding over time, the kind of situation Reinforcement Learning is built for? Answering these questions clearly, before collecting a single piece of data, saves considerable wasted effort later on.
4. Collecting Data

blocks.alt: Multiple sources combine into one dataset

blocks.text: Data collection gathers the raw material every later stage of this workflow ultimately depends on. An existing database or an application's own activity logs are often the most readily available source, since that data already exists and simply needs to be accessed.

A public dataset or a third-party data provider can also be useful, though it needs careful checking for genuine fit to the actual problem being solved. Manual collection or labeling is slow and genuinely expensive, exactly the cost already covered in the Supervised Learning topic, but it is sometimes the only realistic option available.
5. Exploring and Understanding the Data

blocks.alt: Raw data goes through exploratory analysis to produce insights

blocks.text: Exploring and understanding the data comes before any model actually gets built, and it is a genuinely essential stage, not an optional formality. This involves checking for missing values, obvious errors, and unexpected patterns that might indicate a genuine data quality problem.

It also involves understanding what each feature actually means, and how different features relate to each other, building the kind of intuition that makes every later stage considerably more effective. This entire stage gets its own dedicated module later in this course, Exploratory Data Analysis, covering it in genuine, practical depth.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Skipping this exploration stage to jump straight into model training is a common, tempting shortcut that often costs considerably more time later, when a data quality problem surfaces unexpectedly during evaluation instead.

blocks.text: 6. Preparing and Engineering Features

blocks.alt: Cleaned data becomes engineered features, ready for the model

blocks.text: Preparing and engineering features shapes raw data into a form a model can actually learn from effectively. This includes handling missing values, scaling numeric features onto a comparable range, and encoding categorical values into a numeric form a model can actually process.

Each of these specific techniques gets its own dedicated module later in this course, Feature Engineering, Feature Scaling, and Encoding Techniques among them, covering the practical details of exactly how raw, messy real-world data becomes genuinely model-ready.
7. Training and Evaluating a Model

blocks.alt: Training and evaluation repeat until the model is good enough to ship

blocks.text: Choosing and training a model means picking an algorithm that genuinely fits the problem type already decided back in the first stage, then running that algorithm's own training process on the prepared data.

Evaluating the model then asks whether it genuinely performs well, and whether it actually generalizes to new, unseen data, directly echoing the generalization goal already covered in the Supervised Learning topic. A model that only performs well on the exact data it was trained on has not actually succeeded at this stage.
8. This Workflow Is Not Strictly Linear

blocks.alt: Evaluation often sends the process back to data or features rather than moving straight forward

blocks.text: A genuinely important reality about this workflow is that it is not strictly linear in actual practice. Evaluation often reveals a problem that traces back to an earlier stage entirely, poor model performance caused by a genuine data quality issue rather than by the specific model choice itself, for instance.

Going back to an earlier stage and repeating part of the workflow is normal, entirely expected practice in a real project, not a sign that something has gone genuinely wrong. Real Machine Learning work loops back and refines earlier stages constantly, rather than marching through this sequence exactly once from start to finish.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Treating a poor evaluation result as automatically meaning "try a different algorithm" is a common mistake. Very often the actual fix lies back in data quality or feature preparation, not in the model choice itself.

blocks.text: 9. Deployment and Monitoring, Previewed

This connects forward to Model Deployment and Production Machine Learning, both covered in full depth in their own modules later in this course. A model is not actually finished simply because it performs well during evaluation, that is genuinely just the halfway point of a real project.

It still needs to be deployed into an environment where it can actually make useful predictions, monitored to ensure it continues performing well over time, and eventually retrained as real-world conditions inevitably change, exactly the full operational lifecycle covered in genuine depth much later in this course.

blocks.text: 10. Why Understanding This Full Workflow Matters

Understanding this full workflow before diving into any individual stage keeps the later, deeply technical modules of this course connected to the bigger picture. Each specific technique covered ahead, a particular algorithm, a particular preprocessing method, has a clear, specific place within this seven-stage sequence.

It also sets realistic expectations about a real project's actual scope: model training, often the part that gets the most attention and excitement, is genuinely just one stage among several, not the entirety of what a real Machine Learning project actually involves.
11. Worked Example
The example below walks through a small but complete version of this workflow, from raw data through a trained, evaluated model.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score

# Stage 1: problem already defined as Supervised Learning, a classification task
# Stage 2: data collection (simulated here for the example)
rng = np.random.RandomState(42)
X_raw = rng.normal(loc=[50, 5000], scale=[15, 2000], size=(500, 2))  # age, income
y = (X_raw[:, 1] > 6000).astype(int)  # will subscribe: yes/no

# Stage 3: exploring the data (a real project would check distributions, missing values, etc.)
print(f"Data shape: {X_raw.shape}, class balance: {y.mean():.2%} positive")

# Stage 4: preparing features
scaler = StandardScaler()
X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X_raw)

# Stage 5: training a model
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X_scaled, y, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)
model = LogisticRegression()
model.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Stage 6: evaluating the model
test_accuracy = accuracy_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test))
print(f"Test accuracy: {test_accuracy:.2%}")

# Stage 7: deployment and monitoring would follow in a real project, covered later in this course
print("\nModel ready; stages 1 through 6 of the workflow are complete for this example")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: This example deliberately compresses all seven stages into one short script to show the full sequence clearly. A real project spends considerably more time on stages 2 through 4 than this simplified example suggests.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Every real Machine Learning project follows roughly the same repeatable, seven-stage workflow.
The full sequence: define, collect, explore, prepare, train, evaluate, and deploy and monitor.
Defining the problem means deciding which type of Machine Learning fits, shaping every later stage.
Data can come from existing databases, public datasets or providers, or slow, expensive manual collection.
Exploring the data before modeling catches quality problems early, getting its own dedicated module later.
Preparing features shapes raw data into a form a model can learn from, also getting its own dedicated modules.
This workflow is not strictly linear; looping back to refine an earlier stage is normal, expected practice.
A model performing well in evaluation is only the halfway point; deployment and monitoring still follow.
This closes the Introduction to Machine Learning module; next up: Applications of Machine Learning, before moving into Data Collection and Understanding.
